questions.title: ECS Fundamentals — Clusters, Services and Tasks
questions.question: How does AWS ECS work and what are the key concepts for deploying a Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- ECS: managed container orchestration — runs Docker containers on AWS
- Cluster: logical grouping of compute capacity
- Task Definition: blueprint — image, CPU, memory, env vars, ports, volumes
- Service: maintains desired task count; replaces failed tasks; integrates with ALB
- Fargate: serverless compute — no EC2 to manage; AWS manages hosts
- Task Role: IAM role for container's AWS API access
- Execution Role: ECS agent role to pull images from ECR, write logs

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
ECS is Amazon's container orchestration service. You package your Spring Boot application as a Docker container, push it to ECR, and define a Task Definition specifying which image to run, how much CPU and memory to allocate, which ports to expose, and environment variables to inject.

An ECS Service ensures a specified number of task instances are always running. If a task crashes, the service automatically starts a replacement. When deploying a new version, the service does a rolling update — starting new tasks before draining old ones — so deployments are zero-downtime.

Fargate is the mode I recommend for most teams. You never manage EC2 instances — you specify CPU and memory for your containers and AWS handles all host infrastructure. You pay per second of container runtime. EC2 launch type makes sense when you need specific instance types, GPU support, or want to optimize costs for predictable high-volume workloads.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Task Definition (Fargate)

```json
{
  "family": "spring-backend",
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "cpu": "1024",
  "memory": "2048",
  "taskRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456:role/app-task-role",
  "executionRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456:role/ecs-execution-role",
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "spring-api",
    "image": "123456.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/spring-api:abc1234",
    "portMappings": [{"containerPort": 8080}],
    "environment": [
      {"name": "SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE", "value": "prod"}
    ],
    "secrets": [
      {"name": "DB_PASSWORD",
       "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:...:secret:/prod/db-credentials:password::"}
    ],
    "healthCheck": {
      "command": ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -f http://localhost:8080/actuator/health || exit 1"],
      "interval": 30, "timeout": 5, "retries": 3, "startPeriod": 60
    },
    "logConfiguration": {
      "logDriver": "awslogs",
      "options": {
        "awslogs-group": "/ecs/spring-backend",
        "awslogs-region": "ap-south-1",
        "awslogs-stream-prefix": "ecs"
      }
    }
  }]
}
```

## Deploy Rolling Update

```bash
# Register new task definition, update service
aws ecs update-service \
  --cluster prod-cluster \
  --service spring-api \
  --task-definition spring-backend:6 \
  --deployment-configuration 'minimumHealthyPercent=100,maximumPercent=200'
# minimumHealthyPercent=100: never reduce count below desired during deploy
# maximumPercent=200: allow 2x tasks during rollout (old + new running simultaneously)
```

speakable_v2.hook: ECS is Amazon's container orchestration service.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: EC2 launch type makes sense when you need specific instance types, GPU support, or want to optimize costs for predictable high-volume workloads.

questions.title: CI/CD Pipeline for ECS Deployments
questions.question: How do you set up a CI/CD pipeline to automatically deploy a Spring Boot application to ECS?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Pipeline: build → test → Docker build → push ECR → register task def → update service
- Image tagging: git commit SHA for traceability, not 'latest'
- GitHub Actions: aws-actions/* official actions for ECR login, task def update, deploy
- OIDC: GitHub Actions authenticates to AWS without long-lived access keys
- Blue/green: CodeDeploy + ECS for instant rollback capability
- Rollback: update-service back to previous task definition revision

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A typical ECS CI/CD pipeline has four stages: build and test the application, build a Docker image tagged with the git commit SHA, push to ECR, then register a new task definition revision and trigger ECS service update.

Tagging with commit SHA is important for traceability — you always know exactly what code is running in production. With 'latest' tags, two instances with the same tag may run completely different code.

For GitHub Actions, use OIDC authentication instead of long-lived IAM access keys. GitHub's OIDC provider exchanges workflow tokens for temporary AWS credentials scoped to the specific repository and branch. This is far more secure than secrets stored in GitHub.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## GitHub Actions ECS Deploy

```yaml
name: Deploy to ECS
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write  # for OIDC
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { java-version: '21', distribution: 'temurin' }

      - run: mvn -B package -DskipTests=false

      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456:role/github-deploy-role
          aws-region: ap-south-1

      - id: login-ecr
        uses: aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2

      - id: build-image
        env:
          ECR_REGISTRY: ${{ steps.login-ecr.outputs.registry }}
          IMAGE_TAG: ${{ github.sha }}
        run: |
          docker build -t $ECR_REGISTRY/spring-api:$IMAGE_TAG .
          docker push $ECR_REGISTRY/spring-api:$IMAGE_TAG
          echo "image=$ECR_REGISTRY/spring-api:$IMAGE_TAG" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT

      - id: task-def
        uses: aws-actions/amazon-ecs-render-task-definition@v1
        with:
          task-definition: task-definition.json
          container-name: spring-api
          image: ${{ steps.build-image.outputs.image }}

      - uses: aws-actions/amazon-ecs-deploy-task-definition@v1
        with:
          task-definition: ${{ steps.task-def.outputs.task-definition }}
          service: spring-api
          cluster: prod-cluster
          wait-for-service-stability: true
```

speakable_v2.hook: A typical ECS CI/CD pipeline has four stages: build and test the application, build a Docker image tagged with the git commit SHA, push to ECR, then register a new task definition revision and trigger.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This is far more secure than secrets stored in GitHub.

questions.title: ECS Auto-Scaling
questions.question: How do you configure auto-scaling for ECS services based on CPU, memory, and request metrics?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Application Auto Scaling: scale ECS service desired count up/down automatically
- Target tracking: maintain average CPU at 70% — AWS adjusts task count
- Step scaling: scale by specific amounts at threshold boundaries
- Scheduled scaling: pre-scale before predictable load spikes
- Scale-in protection: prevent terminating tasks processing long jobs
- ALB request count: scale on RequestCountPerTarget if better than CPU
- Scale-out fast, scale-in slow: asymmetric cooldown (300s out, 600s in)
- Minimum/maximum: guard rails on task count

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
ECS services scale through Application Auto Scaling, which adjusts the desired task count based on CloudWatch metrics. Target tracking is the simplest policy — you define a target metric value like 70% average CPU utilization, and AWS automatically adds or removes tasks to maintain that target. It's similar to a thermostat.

I prefer scaling on ALB request count per target rather than CPU for API services. CPU utilization can be misleading — some requests are CPU-intensive while others are mostly waiting for database responses. Requests per target directly reflects the load each task is handling.

Scale-out should happen fast, scale-in should be slow. You don't want tasks terminated while they're processing requests. A 60-second scale-out cooldown with a 300-second scale-in cooldown is a common configuration. For services with long-running jobs, enable scale-in protection on tasks that are actively processing.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Target Tracking Auto Scaling

```bash
# Register ECS service as scalable target
aws application-autoscaling register-scalable-target \
  --service-namespace ecs \
  --scalable-dimension ecs:service:DesiredCount \
  --resource-id service/prod-cluster/spring-api \
  --min-capacity 2 \
  --max-capacity 10

# CPU-based target tracking: maintain 70% average CPU
aws application-autoscaling put-scaling-policy \
  --policy-name cpu-target-tracking \
  --service-namespace ecs \
  --scalable-dimension ecs:service:DesiredCount \
  --resource-id service/prod-cluster/spring-api \
  --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-scaling-policy-configuration '{
    "TargetValue": 70.0,
    "PredefinedMetricSpecification": {
      "PredefinedMetricType": "ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization"
    },
    "ScaleOutCooldown": 60,
    "ScaleInCooldown": 300
  }'

# ALB request count per target (often better metric)
--target-tracking-scaling-policy-configuration '{
  "TargetValue": 1000.0,
  "PredefinedMetricSpecification": {
    "PredefinedMetricType": "ALBRequestCountPerTarget",
    "ResourceLabel": "app/prod-alb/xxx/targetgroup/spring-api/yyy"
  }
}'
```

## Scheduled Scaling

```bash
# Pre-scale before Monday morning traffic spike
aws application-autoscaling put-scheduled-action \
  --service-namespace ecs \
  --scalable-dimension ecs:service:DesiredCount \
  --resource-id service/prod-cluster/spring-api \
  --scheduled-action-name scale-up-monday-morning \
  --schedule "cron(0 8 ? * MON *)" \
  --scalable-target-action '{"MinCapacity": 5, "MaxCapacity": 15}'

# Scale back down Monday night
aws application-autoscaling put-scheduled-action \
  --scheduled-action-name scale-down-night \
  --schedule "cron(0 22 * * ? *)" \
  --scalable-target-action '{"MinCapacity": 2, "MaxCapacity": 10}'
```

speakable_v2.hook: ECS services scale through Application Auto Scaling, which adjusts the desired task count based on CloudWatch metrics.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: For services with long-running jobs, enable scale-in protection on tasks that are actively processing.

questions.title: ECS Networking and Security
questions.question: How do you secure ECS tasks with VPC networking, security groups, and IAM task roles?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- awsvpc network mode: each Fargate task gets its own ENI and private IP — no port conflicts
- Security groups on tasks: inbound from ALB security group only; outbound to DB, external APIs
- Private subnets: Fargate tasks in private subnets — no direct internet access
- NAT Gateway: outbound internet from private subnets (for pulling Docker images, external APIs)
- Task role: minimum permissions to AWS services (S3, SES, Secrets Manager)
- Execution role: ECS agent pulls image from ECR, gets secrets, writes logs
- Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store: Secrets Manager for credentials; encrypted at rest
- Service Connect: service-to-service discovery within ECS cluster

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
In Fargate with awsvpc networking, each task gets its own elastic network interface with a private IP address. This means you can apply security groups directly to tasks, not just to EC2 instances. The right pattern is to allow inbound traffic to the task only from the ALB's security group, and restrict outbound to only what the application actually needs — the database security group, specific external API endpoints.

Fargate tasks should run in private subnets with no direct internet access. They connect outbound through a NAT Gateway for pulling Docker images and calling external APIs, but they're not directly reachable from the internet — all traffic comes in through the ALB.

The task role is the IAM identity for your application code. It should have only the permissions your app actually needs — for example, read access to specific S3 buckets, permission to send emails via SES, read access to specific Secrets Manager secrets. The execution role is different — it's used by the ECS agent itself to pull the container image from ECR and write logs to CloudWatch.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## VPC Architecture for ECS

```
VPC (10.0.0.0/16)
│
├── Public Subnets (10.0.1.0/24, 10.0.2.0/24)
│   ├── ALB (internet-facing)         ← internet traffic enters here
│   └── NAT Gateway                   ← outbound internet for private subnets
│
└── Private Subnets (10.0.10.0/24, 10.0.20.0/24)
    ├── ECS Fargate Tasks             ← Spring Boot containers here
    │   └── Security Group: inbound 8080 from ALB SG only
    └── RDS PostgreSQL                ← Database here
        └── Security Group: inbound 5432 from ECS Task SG only
```

## Task Role — Least Privilege

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-uploads/*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["secretsmanager:GetSecretValue"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-south-1:123456:secret:/prod/myapp/*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["ses:SendEmail"],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {"StringEquals": {"ses:FromAddress": "noreply@myapp.com"}}
    }
  ]
}
```

## Security Groups

```bash
# ALB security group: accepts internet traffic
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-alb \
  --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

# ECS task security group: accepts ONLY from ALB
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-ecs-tasks \
  --protocol tcp --port 8080 --source-group sg-alb

# RDS security group: accepts ONLY from ECS tasks
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-id sg-rds \
  --protocol tcp --port 5432 --source-group sg-ecs-tasks
```

speakable_v2.hook: In Fargate with awsvpc networking, each task gets its own elastic network interface with a private IP address.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: The execution role is different — it's used by the ECS agent itself to pull the container image from ECR and write logs to CloudWatch.

questions.title: ECS Secrets and Environment Configuration
questions.question: How do you securely manage environment variables and secrets for ECS tasks?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Never hardcode credentials in task definitions or Docker images
- Secrets Manager: for credentials (DB passwords, API keys) — auto-rotation support
- Parameter Store: for non-secret config (feature flags, URLs) — cheaper than Secrets Manager
- secrets in task definition: ECS injects at task startup — value fetched from Secrets Manager
- environment in task definition: plain text — only for non-sensitive values
- Encryption: Secrets Manager encrypts at rest with KMS key
- Spring profiles: map SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE env var to profile-specific config
- SSM Parameter Store with Spring Cloud AWS: auto-load app config from Parameter Store

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The rule is simple: credentials never go in plaintext. Database passwords, API keys, and certificates always go into AWS Secrets Manager. Task definitions reference the Secrets Manager ARN, and ECS injects the value as an environment variable at task startup. The application code reads it from the environment exactly like any other variable — there's no SDK call needed in application code.

For non-sensitive configuration like service URLs, feature flag values, and timeouts, AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store is more cost-effective. Both are injected at container startup the same way.

The task's execution role needs GetSecretValue permission on the specific secrets it uses. Following least privilege, the role should specify exact ARNs, not wildcards, so a compromised task can only access its own secrets.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Task Definition Secrets Injection

```json
{
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "spring-api",
    "image": "123456.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/spring-api:abc1234",
    
    "environment": [
      {"name": "SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE", "value": "prod"},
      {"name": "SERVER_PORT", "value": "8080"},
      {"name": "APP_FEATURE_NEW_UI", "value": "true"}
    ],
    
    "secrets": [
      {
        "name": "SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD",
        "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-south-1:123456:secret:/prod/myapp/db:password::"
      },
      {
        "name": "STRIPE_SECRET_KEY",
        "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:ap-south-1:123456:secret:/prod/myapp/stripe:apiKey::"
      },
      {
        "name": "REDIS_PASSWORD",
        "valueFrom": "arn:aws:ssm:ap-south-1:123456:parameter/prod/myapp/redis/password"
      }
    ]
  }]
}
```

## Spring Cloud AWS — Auto-Load Parameter Store

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.awspring.cloud</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-cloud-aws-starter-parameter-store</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  config:
    import: "aws-parameterstore:"
  cloud:
    aws:
      parameterstore:
        prefix: /prod/myapp
        # Loads /prod/myapp/config.* as Spring properties automatically
```

```bash
# Store config in Parameter Store
aws ssm put-parameter \
  --name /prod/myapp/spring.datasource.url \
  --value "jdbc:postgresql://prod-db.cluster.ap-south-1.rds.amazonaws.com:5432/appdb" \
  --type String

aws ssm put-parameter \
  --name /prod/myapp/spring.data.redis.host \
  --value "prod-cache.xxxxx.cache.amazonaws.com" \
  --type String
```

speakable_v2.hook: The rule is simple: credentials never go in plaintext.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Following least privilege, the role should specify exact ARNs, not wildcards, so a compromised task can only access its own secrets.

questions.title: ECS Logging and Observability
questions.question: How do you set up logging, metrics, and monitoring for ECS-deployed Spring Boot applications?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- awslogs driver: route container stdout/stderr to CloudWatch Logs
- Structured logging: JSON format — easier to query in CloudWatch Insights
- CloudWatch Logs Insights: query logs with SQL-like syntax
- Spring Boot Actuator: /health endpoint for ECS health check
- Container Insights: cluster-level CPU, memory, network metrics per task/service
- X-Ray: distributed tracing — trace requests across microservices
- CloudWatch Alarms: alert on CPU, memory, error rate, response time
- Log retention: set retention policy — logs are free to store but cost to query

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The standard ECS logging setup is the awslogs driver configured in the task definition. Container stdout and stderr are automatically streamed to a CloudWatch Logs log group. Spring Boot applications should log in JSON format so CloudWatch Logs Insights can parse and query individual fields — find all 500 errors, group by endpoint, calculate 95th percentile response times.

For the ECS health check, point it at Spring Boot Actuator's /actuator/health endpoint. ECS uses this to decide whether a task is healthy. An unhealthy task is replaced automatically. Configure a startPeriod of 60 seconds to give Spring Boot time to initialize before health checks begin counting failures.

Container Insights gives you cluster-level visibility — CPU and memory per service, per task, per container. Enable it on the cluster with a single setting. For request-level tracing across microservices, AWS X-Ray integrated with the Spring Boot Actuator instrumentation shows you the full call tree for a request, including time spent in each downstream service.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Task Definition Logging Config

```json
{
  "logConfiguration": {
    "logDriver": "awslogs",
    "options": {
      "awslogs-group": "/ecs/prod/spring-api",
      "awslogs-region": "ap-south-1",
      "awslogs-stream-prefix": "ecs",
      "awslogs-create-group": "true"
    }
  }
}
```

## Structured JSON Logging in Spring Boot

```xml
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>net.logstash.logback</groupId>
    <artifactId>logstash-logback-encoder</artifactId>
    <version>7.4</version>
</dependency>
```

```xml
<!-- logback-spring.xml -->
<appender name="STDOUT" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
    <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
        <!-- Outputs: {"timestamp":"...","level":"INFO","logger":"...","message":"...","traceId":"..."} -->
        <customFields>{"service":"spring-api","environment":"prod"}</customFields>
    </encoder>
</appender>
```

## CloudWatch Logs Insights Queries

```sql
-- Find all 5xx errors in last hour
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter level = "ERROR" and statusCode >= 500
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 50

-- Average response time per endpoint
fields @timestamp, endpoint, responseTimeMs
| stats avg(responseTimeMs) as avgMs, count() as requests by endpoint
| sort avgMs desc

-- Error rate by service
filter level = "ERROR"
| stats count() as errors by bin(5m)
| sort @timestamp
```

## CloudWatch Alarm for Error Rate

```bash
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name spring-api-error-rate \
  --metric-name ErrorCount \
  --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB \
  --dimensions Name=LoadBalancer,Value=app/prod-alb/xxx \
  --statistic Sum \
  --period 60 \
  --threshold 10 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --evaluation-periods 3 \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:ap-south-1:123456:engineering-alerts
```

speakable_v2.hook: The standard ECS logging setup is the awslogs driver configured in the task definition.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.
